title: What Scripture Calls the Father’s It Also Calls the Son’s and the Spirit’s
english: … I make known to you that no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). And again: “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are judged spiritually. But the spiritual man judges everyone, while he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:14–16). And again: “Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:1–2).
That for the same cause, the one essence of the Trinity, Scripture says at one time that things are the Father’s and at another that the same things are the Son’s or the Holy Spirit’s.

Scripture, making plain that there is one Godhead and one lordship, says at one time that certain things are the Father’s, and at another declares that they belong to the Son or to the Holy Spirit. So it is when the Savior says to the Jews in Matthew: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). So it is too when the renowned Paul writes to the Philippians: “For all seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21); and to the Galatians: “And those who are Christ Jesus’s have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5:24); and to the Corinthians: “For the love of Christ holds us fast, since we have judged this: he died for all, that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). And again: “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14). And again: “Be zealous for the things of the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 14:1).

The Church, too, understood together with the glory sent up within it and the bloodless worship offered there, he declared to be God’s, writing to the Corinthians the first time in this way: “Give no offence to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God” (1 Corinthians 10:32); and again: “We have no such custom, nor do the churches of God” (1 Corinthians 11:16). But writing to the Ephesians in turn, he taught that it is Christ’s, saying: “that he might present the church to himself blameless, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that it might be holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27). If he did not think so, let someone explain what the prophet Haggai means when he says that “great shall be the latter glory of this house, beyond the former” (Haggai 2:9): that is, the glory of the Church of Christ and of the praise given in it, beyond the synagogue of the Jews, in which God the Father alone was confessed as God and glorified.

Following on, then, he says that the gospel too is at one time God the Father’s, writing to the Romans: “Paul, a slave of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God” (Romans 1:1); and again: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed; and the righteous shall live by faith” (Romans 1:16–17); and to the Corinthians, the second time: “that I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge” (2 Corinthians 11:7). At another time he writes that it is the only-begotten God’s. To the Corinthians, the first time: “But we did not make use of this right; we bear all things, so as not to put any hindrance in the way of the gospel of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:12); and the second time: “When I came to Troas for the gospel of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:12); and again: “glorifying God for the submission of your confession to the gospel of Christ” (2 Corinthians 9:13); and to the Romans: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in the gospel of his Son” (Romans 1:9).

He also said that the sacred ministry is performed at one time for God the Father and at another for God his only-begotten Son, writing to the Corinthians the first time: “Let a man regard us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover it is required of stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:1–2); and the second time: “in everything commending ourselves as ministers of God” (2 Corinthians 6:4); and again: “Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one beside himself: I am more” (2 Corinthians 11:23). And [...]

[...] “Who trusted in the Lord and was put to shame? Or who held fast in his fear and was forsaken? Or who called upon him, and he overlooked him?” (Sirach 2:10). For, as even those outside say, whoever obeys God, him he gladly hears. Accordingly, that nothing in himself is acquired or worked in him by another, but that from his own store …

title: All That the Father Has Is the Son’s
english: … he brings in all good things. This he shows by giving, with authority, the one divine peace, of which “there is no end” (Isaiah 9:7), and of which Isaiah cried aloud: “O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us all things. O Lord, we know no other besides you” (Isaiah 26:12–13). He gives it as his own, because nature and lordship are held in common. For he said: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27).

That is why Paul too, and not least, said that both uncreated hypostases supply this God-given gift without any difference, writing to the Romans somewhere in these words: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7). And this saying too has given us to discern that the matter stands so: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). For no one who is not ignorant takes these words of the creation; they are taken of the divine rank, if one must speak of rank in the case of God.

“For the Father,” he says, “is God. So am I, for I am his only-begotten, true and beloved Son. The Father is Lord. I too am Lord of all, and heir of a living Father, master of the inheritance. I inherit what is his, partly as its maker and partly as his true-born Son; but I was appointed heir as one who became man. The Father is Creator and King. So am I, for I told you that ‘there was a certain king, and he went to make a wedding feast for his son the king’ (Matthew 22:2). The Father is unchangeable. So am I, for it has been prophesied of me: ‘You are the same, and your years will not fail’ (Psalm 102:27). The Father is impassible. So am I, so that those who share in me also partake of impassibility. The Father is without beginning. So am I. For there was never a time when he did not have the name of Father, and did not have me, the subsisting radiance of his glory, the ‘exact imprint of his hypostasis’ (Hebrews 1:3) and the ‘image of the Godhead.’ Life and light and goodness and power and wisdom and truth, and all that is worthy of God: this the Father is. So am I, as you have already heard. And indeed I too am Savior, ‘making the sun rise on the righteous and on sinners’ (Matthew 5:45), and not bringing ‘evil for evil.’ The Father loves mankind. So do I, since for your sake ‘I emptied myself, taking the form of a slave’ (Philippians 2:7), and bore with you as you struck me, spat on me, mocked me and crucified me.”

So he said that all the Father’s attributes are his, so as to grant God the Father nothing more than this alone: to be Father of a Son who is without beginning together with him and subsists together with him. This saying too persuades us to believe so: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them” (John 17:10). For if this was not said because of their natural relation, and if the Son has not been glorified in his essence with all that is the Father’s, if there is not one kingdom and one lordship, then, by heretical reasoning at least, there are things that fall not under the Father’s authority but under the Son’s.

And again: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me” (John 8:54). “When I speak to you,” he says, “of my own divine glory, that ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), you do not believe. But there is the Father who bears witness to me that I am glorified by nature, since I am his beloved and true Son, and your God and Master.” Then he says: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you” (John 17:1). Here too equal honor and glory are kept for the divine hypostases. For in whatever way we take the Father to glorify his Son, in that same way he himself is glorified by him.

And again he goes on: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself with the glory that I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5). It is dreadful to hear: he who has glory without beginning with his own Father, for this is what “with the glory that I had before the world was” means, is not glorified by heretics. And what was this glory? The one that Mark too, I think, spoke of: “when the Son comes in the glory of his Father” (Mark 8:38), which is to say: he has the Father’s glory, and in it he will come the second time. And those whose glory is one do not have one Godhead, kingdom and worship here and another there. Hence he charges them beforehand: “Believe in God, and believe in me. In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:1–2). “For since the Godhead,” he says, “admits no difference, you must hold one knowledge of faith concerning the Trinity, so that in this way you may dwell in those thrice-blessed courts, which are fitting and sufficient for all.”
So, granting not only what a teacher grants but also what God grants, he says: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5:20). Here too you notice his sovereign freedom: that, as it were, …

title: Equality of Father and Son
english: … does not plead with one greater, but forgives as sovereign.

Matthew too, adding his own share to what is taught of the only-begotten Son as God, said: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father” (Matthew 11:27). How then do these men quarrel as though they knew the Father to be incomparable, his Son to be unlike him, and his essence to be unbegottenness? They leave nothing as the special preserve of the knowledge that belongs to God the Father and the only-begotten God, and they do not reckon that nothing of a different nature has a knowledge equal to that of a being whose essence is other than its own.

Paul likewise writes to Timothy in the first letter: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who bore witness to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment spotless and blameless until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only Mighty One will show, the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one among men has seen or can see; to whom be honor and eternal glory to the ages of ages. Amen” (1 Timothy 6:13–16). The heretics have resolved to give to the Father alone the words “the only Mighty One and King of those who reign” and what follows. But just as Paul spoke of both the ever-remembered hypostases, “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus,” so he sang the praises that follow of both of them, as of one in Godhead. For he was not ignorant, as these men are, of “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15), and “that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23), and “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20), and “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him” (Baruch 3:35), and “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17).

Rather, the words set out here point more toward the Son. For the text runs: “to keep the commandment until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only Mighty One will show” (1 Timothy 6:14–15). And it is plain that the Son will show his own appearing when he comes the second time. Observe, then, that Paul assigns to him the first glory too.

And to the Romans: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, both his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20). These words too, because Father and Son are equal in honor, do not tilt toward a thing made. For the Creator’s being understood as begotten does not keep his eternity and divinity from being known, that is, his Godhead, which is always and in the same way. And to the Philippians: “Who, being in the form of God, did not count being equal to God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave” (Philippians 2:6–7).

What in this equality is found unequal? “He did not seize it,” Paul says; he did not take to himself his being equal by nature to God the Father. And indeed he who was emptied by no one else, but emptied himself, showed himself to be at once Master in his own right and eternal. For if he came to be in the form of a slave, it is beyond dispute that before this happened he did not dwell among things made, but was in the free nature of the Father. Since he could not be seen, he came down, without change and not in mere appearance, as far as the form of a household slave. He thrust off the slave’s burdens and gave the beginning of a brighter life; and so he who was without beginning came to be known.

As for the other things written to these same Philippians, in which Paul already shows in some way, as far as the unintelligent need it, that the Son is pre-eminent and supreme together with his own Father, I have already spoken of them above, in the seventh chapter. But nothing prevents our establishing this from the ancient Scripture as well, for theology must not be handled in passing. So God says in Isaiah: “Your new moons and sabbaths and your feasts my soul hates. You have become a surfeit to me; I will no longer let your sins go. Even if you make your prayer full, I will not hear you, for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, become clean, take away your sins from your souls” (Isaiah 1:13–16).

You see, then, that his love for mankind runs ahead even of his threat: he is all but reconciled already, and does not know how to keep his anger long, or rather how to be angry at all. He hates their feasts, that is, their worship, because it falls short of the most perfect knowledge of God; and he bids them be baptized, so as to receive the faith according to the Master’s ordinance for baptism.
